newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Cautious Morocco steps on path to reform.
newsitem.headline: Cautious Morocco steps on path to reform.

text.p: Urged on by King Hassan, traditionally cautious Morocco is starting an experiment to extend democracy which could break the centre-right's stranglehold on power.

Diplomats and political commentators said on Sunday that the overwhelming vote -- 99.56 percent -- in favour of changing the constitution in last Friday's referendum opened the door to two major changes:
-- providing the opposition chance of a majority voice for the first time in three decades of centre-right party rule;
-- giving disadvantaged rural people, who form nearly half the population of 27 million, more say in what happens in the North African country.
The government is to start this week looking at the changes which, for the first time since independence in 1956, had the backing of the main opposition parties.

The reforms will create two houses of parliament. The lower will be directly elected, the upper one will be indirectly elected and have power to force a vote of no-confidence in the government and topple it.
"There is still much more to do, sorting out detail of the electoral laws...And these will be even more important than the referendum," said one Western diplomat.
"But the change will bring more democracy if the authorities don't interfere in the indirect elections."
It was fear of this that impelled a handful of dissenters to call for a boycott of the vote -- seeing the upper house as being able to sabotage policy of an elected government.
The main opposition, known as the Koutla (democratic bloc), believes indirect elections of one-third of members in the current 333-seat parliament thwarted it in the last poll.
But despite reservations, Koutla's main parties, the old- guard Istiqlal and Socialist Union of People's Forces, threw their weight behind change and urged a 'yes' vote.

"The essential thing is tht it (the vote) has removed the distance between opposition and government for the first time, and this is good for the country's unity and stability," said Ahmed el-Kohen, a sociologist and university professor.
Traditional allegiance to King Hassan, who proposed the reforms, weighed heavily in the 'yes' vote from the over 10 million people who took part out of an eligible 12.3 million.

Former human rights minister Mohamed Ziyane, an outspoken lawyer who voted 'yes', said: "People voted yes through fidelity towards King Hassan...In Morocco we vote by respect and loyalty to the king, nothing else counted after he called publicly for a yes vote."

Members of the new upper house will be elected mainly through professional bodies, unions and local councils, which Interior Minister Driss Basri said on Saturday would "correct the regional disparities" for development.

Rabat has no illusions about the imbalance between town and country. Earlier this year a report drawn up with the United Nations depicted the poverty, illiteracy and hardships of life in the Moroccan countryside.

Morocco's countrydwellers contribute massively to foreign exchange earnings through farm produce. Yet the report pointed out that "out of 1.8 million people receiving less than $230 a year, it is estimated that 80 percent come from rural areas."
Tied into regional growth will be a series of "Development Plans" to be worked out by a Higher Council of National Promotion and Planning.
At the same time, the government accounting office will become a "constitutional institution" to impose tighter control over finance bills and public spending.
One diplomat cautioned that while there was need for tight spending control the new body could undermine some government plans if it chose to oppose them and question their financing.
The complexities of new laws mean that changes in the electoral process are unlikely before next June and there is no public timetable for the other reforms.
